title: Checks-Effects-Interactions Pattern
content: The Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern is the standard defense against reentrancy in Solidity. A function should first run all validations (checks), then update its own storage (effects), and only afterwards call external contracts (interactions). Reordering the pattern, for example sending funds before zeroing a balance, lets a malicious recipient call back into the contract and repeat the withdrawal before the state settles.

title: Read-Only Reentrancy
content: Read-only reentrancy is a newer twist on the classic attack: the vulnerable contract is only called as a view/pure read by another protocol, so it appears safe, but the attacker re-enters the read path after mutating state in a separate call. Cross-contract accounting bugs of this kind have drained lending and vault protocols. Auditors now check not just write functions but every external read that feeds an economic decision.

title: Withdrawal Pattern vs Push Payments
content: Smart contracts should let users pull funds (withdrawal pattern) instead of pushing payments to them. Push-style transfers using transfer/send can fail silently on gas or call-depth limits and give a griefing recipient the ability to block a contract; pull-based design lets each user withdraw their own balance and keeps the contract resilient. The withdraw function still needs CEI ordering and a check that the external call succeeded.

title: tx.origin Authorization Misuse
content: Using tx.origin for authorization is a well-known Solidity pitfall: tx.origin returns the original account that started the transaction, not the immediate caller, so a phishing contract can call a wallet function and pass the wallet-owner check. msg.sender is the direct caller and is safe for role checks; tx.origin should only be used for explicit anti-phishing conditions, never as an access-control primitive.

title: Insecure On-Chain Randomness
content: Ethereum has no native source of true randomness, so naive contracts derive it from block attributes like blockhash or prevrandao. Block proposers can bias or predict these values, letting them win lotteries, raffles, or NFT mints that rely on the random draw. Secure designs use commit-reveal schemes, external VDFs/beacon oracles, or verifiable random functions with delayed reveal windows.

title: Unchecked External Call Return Values
content: Low-level Solidity calls (call, delegatecall, send) return a success boolean instead of reverting. Ignoring that boolean lets a contract continue as if a transfer or sub-call succeeded when it actually failed, corrupting accounting. Always require(success) or handle the failure branch explicitly; using high-level calls on an interface surfaces errors automatically.

title: delegatecall to Untrusted Callee
content: delegatecall executes code in the caller's storage context, so pointing it at an untrusted address lets that address rewrite any storage variable, including owners and balances. The Parity wallet hack destroyed millions of ETH through an unprotected delegatecall. Guard the target address, keep proxy storage collision-free, and never let users supply arbitrary delegatecall targets.

title: State Variable Shadowing
content: Shadowing occurs when a derived contract declares a variable with the same name as one in a base contract; the two occupy different storage slots and code may read the wrong one. It typically appears in inheritance-heavy or upgradeable setups and can break balances or settings silently. Solidity's compiler flags and modern linting tools detect most shadowing cases.

title: Missing Access Control on Privileged Functions
content: Access-control failures rank first in OWASP's smart-contract top 10: functions that mint, set fees, pause, or upgrade are left callable by anyone because the owner/admin modifier is missing. In 2024-2025 incident data, access-control flaws caused the largest dollar losses of any vulnerability class. Every state-changing admin function needs an explicit role check and a test that unprivileged callers revert.

title: Proxy Upgrade Storage Collision
content: Upgradeable contracts store implementation logic behind a proxy, but if a new implementation declares a variable that occupies a slot already used by the proxy or an earlier implementation, values silently corrupt. Storage-layout checks and structured proxy patterns (EIP-1967, transparent proxies) prevent collisions. Upgrades should also be governed by timelocks and tested against the full storage layout.

title: Proxy Initializer and Reinitialization
content: Proxies cannot run constructors, so upgradeable contracts use an initialize() function guarded by an initializer modifier. If the guard is missing or the address owner check is weak, anyone can call initialize() on an uninitialized proxy and claim ownership, as seen in several exploit chains. Modern patterns also protect against reinitialization of logic contracts themselves.

title: Denial of Service via Block Gas Limit
content: Contracts that loop over unbounded arrays, or let users push entries to storage that later functions must iterate, can hit the block gas limit and become permanently unusable. An attacker can also grief by making the only path to funds fail (DoS with failed call). Bounded loops, pagination, and pull-based withdrawals prevent gas-exhaustion denial of service.

title: Signature Replay and Cross-Chain Replay
content: Signed messages are only as scoped as their domain: if a signature does not bind the chain id, contract address, and nonce, the same signature can be replayed on another chain or in a second call. EIP-712 typed data includes domain separators precisely to stop cross-chain replay. Signature malleability (two valid encodings of one signature) is mitigated by using the lower-s form and validating against the recovered address.

title: Single-Source Spot Oracle Manipulation
content: Protocols that price assets from one shallow AMM pool let an attacker move the pool price with a large swap and then borrow, liquidate, or settle against the distorted quote. Robust designs use time-weighted average prices (TWAP), multiple independent feeds, or external oracles with deviation thresholds. Oracle-manipulation losses are consistently among the top DeFi attack vectors.

title: Flash Loan Amplification of Bugs
content: Flash loans are uncollateralized loans repaid within the same transaction; they do not cause losses by themselves but let attackers magnify small pricing or logic bugs into large drains by deploying huge capital for one block. Many major exploits are a small arithmetic or oracle flaw amplified by a flash loan. Audits must consider worst-case single-transaction capital.

title: Governance Attack Mechanics
content: On-chain governance can be subverted without touching code: an attacker buys enough tokens to pass a malicious proposal, or passes a treasury transfer buried inside a low-turnout vote. Quorum manipulation, proposal spam, and vote-buying are all real vectors; timelocks and emergency pauses exist to give the community a window to respond before funds move.

title: Admin / Deployer Key Exploits
content: Many of the largest losses bypass code entirely and target the keys that control it: compromised deployer wallets, hot signing keys, or single-signer admin functions that can pause, mint, or move funds. Incident data shows key and signer compromise now rivals smart-contract bugs. Mitigations: multisig with hardware signers, timelocks, separate cold wallets for governance, and monitoring of signer activity.

title: ERC-4626 Vault Share Inflation Attack
content: Tokenized vaults (ERC-4626) that compute shares from a donation-inflatable balance can be attacked on first deposit: a tiny first deposit, then a large donation, leaves subsequent depositors with nearly worthless shares. Mitigations include virtual offset shares, a minimum initial deposit, or accruing fees on the first mint. This class of accounting bug has been exploited in real yield vaults.

title: Concentrated Liquidity (Uniswap v3-style)
content: Concentrated liquidity lets liquidity providers allocate capital to a chosen price range instead of the full curve, earning higher fees but taking higher impermanent-loss risk when price leaves the range. Positions become an NFT with custom ticks, and active ranges can be targeted by MEV. AMM design choices like this directly shape where hacks and sandwishes occur.

title: AMM Hook Failure Patterns (Uniswap v4-style)
content: Hooks let third parties run code at specific points of an AMM swap lifecycle (before/after swap, liquidity, position changes). Trail of Bits found recurring failure patterns in hook code: missing caller checks, incorrect tick math, accounting bugs that still satisfy the pool invariant, and hooks that break atomicity. Any code that runs inside a pool must be treated as part of the trust boundary.

title: Liquidation Cascades in Lending Markets
content: When a large borrower approaches insolvency, liquidators race to close the position, and each liquidation sells collateral and pushes prices further, triggering more liquidations. Cascades can crash collateral prices and leave the lending protocol undercollateralized. Health-factor thresholds, price-change bounds, and partial liquidations are designed to dampen this spiral.

title: veTokenomics and Vote Bribery
content: Vote-escrowed tokens (veTokens) lock tokens for voting power over gauge emissions; the resulting 'veToken wars' create markets where protocols bribe voters to direct rewards. Bribing is not itself an exploit, but it skews capital allocation and can be used to pump specific pools. Analysts monitor bribe flows as an indicator of where yield is being manufactured rather than earned.

title: Stablecoin Depeg Mechanics
content: Stablecoins hold parity through mechanisms ranging from fiat reserves (USDT/USDC) to algorithmic supply adjustments and overcollateralized CDPs (DAI). Depegs happen when reserves are questioned, collateral falls, or the arb loop that restores parity breaks. A depeg can cascade into lending markets because stablecoins back most borrowing.

title: Fee-on-Transfer and Deflationary Tokens vs AMMs
content: Tokens that deduct a fee or burn on every transfer break constant-product AMM accounting because the pool receives less than the stated amount while the swap math assumes the full amount. Rebasing tokens create similar drift. Integrations must measure post-transfer balances and update reserves accordingly, otherwise arbitrageurs can drain the pool.

title: Bridge Security Models
content: Bridges move assets across chains using different trust models: lock-and-mint with validator sets, optimistic bridges with challenge periods, and light-client/zero-knowledge proof systems. Validator-compromise and signature-threshold failures have been the most expensive bridge attacks (two-thirds of bridge validators can authorize a fraudulent withdrawal). The security of a bridge equals the security of its weakest trust component.

title: Reward Farming and Sybil Abuse
content: Yield programs that pay per address or per liquidity are farmed by sybils that split funds across many wallets, borrow to farm, or self-pair liquidity to capture rewards with minimal risk. Farming abuse distorts TVL and volume metrics and can drain treasury rewards. Programs counter it with lockups, quadratic or reputation-weighted distributions, and wash-trade detection.

title: MEV Types: Arbitrage, Sandwich, Liquidation
content: Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) is profit extracted by reordering, including, or excluding transactions within a block. The main types are DEX arbitrage (balancing prices across pools), sandwich attacks (frontrunning a victim swap with a buy, then selling after it pushes price up), and liquidation MEV (racing to liquidate underwater positions for the bonus). Each type has distinct on-chain signatures.

title: Atomic Bundles and Searchers
content: Flashbots and similar infrastructure let MEV searchers submit atomic bundles: sequences of transactions that execute together or not at all, letting a searcher safely frontrun a victim trade and backrun it in the same block without losing to another bot. This professionalized MEV shifted extraction from public-mempool bidding wars into private order-flow auctions where the block builder selects the most profitable bundle.

title: Private Order Flow and Proposer-Builder Separation
content: Private order flow routes user transactions directly to builders, bypassing the public mempool, which reduces frontrunning but concentrates MEV knowledge in a few entities. Proposer-Builder Separation (PBS) splits block proposal from block building so validators cannot easily extract MEV themselves and competition happens in the builder market. These mechanisms determine who captures the value users create.

title: Composability and Cross-Contract Risk
content: DeFi protocols compose like lego bricks, so a bug in one contract can be reached from many others: a flash loan from A, a swap through B, a deposit into C, a withdrawal from D in a single transaction. This composability amplifies exploit blast radius and makes isolated audits insufficient; security review must model the full dependency graph.

title: Restaking and Shared-Security Risks
content: Restaking lets staked ETH secure additional networks (AVS) in exchange for extra yield. The risk is economic layering: the same underlying stake backs many services, so a failure in one AVS can cascade into slashing that drains the base layer. Yield chasing in restaking has become a significant systemic-risk topic for 2025-2026.

title: Prediction Markets
content: Prediction markets let traders buy shares in outcomes (e.g. 'Will BTC be above X on date Y') with prices that continuously imply probabilities. Major platforms (Polymarket, Kalshi) run order books on CLOB or CTF-style exchanges and resolve via oracle/reporter disputes after the event. Prices are studied as real-time probabilistic forecasts and can move faster than polling or expert opinion.

title: Prediction Market Resolution and Disputes
content: The payout of a prediction market depends on how the outcome is resolved: a UMA-style optimistic oracle, a reporter token staking game, or a centralized adjudicator. Resolution disputes, long-tail ambiguity, and oracle manipulation are the key structural risks. A market is only as credible as its resolution mechanism, which is why some platforms restrict markets to unambiguous binary outcomes.

title: Prediction Markets as Information Aggregators
content: Because traders put money behind beliefs, prediction-market prices aggregate dispersed information and penalize noise; this 'wisdom of crowds' property makes them more accurate than polls for many geopolitical and financial events. The efficient-market intuition applies: prices reflect the marginal trader's view, so sudden moves often signal new information entering the market.

title: Wash Trading Detection
content: Wash trading is self-dealing that fakes volume: the same entity buys and sells to itself, or two colluding parties cross trades. On-chain it is detectable via shared funding sources, repetitive trade patterns, and volume that is uncorrelated with unique trader counts. Wash trading inflates volume rankings and misleads momentum signals, so volume quality must be adjusted for it.

title: Spoofing and Layering in Order Books
content: Spoofing places large non-bona-fide orders to create false support or resistance, then cancels them before execution; layering stacks many such orders across price levels. Both manipulate perceived depth to move price or trigger stops. Regulators have fined firms billions for spoofing in traditional markets, and crypto CEXs now apply similar detection heuristics.

title: Market Making and Inventory Risk
content: A market maker continuously quotes bids and asks to earn the spread while managing the risk of holding inventory in a moving market. If price trends against the position, spread revenue can be wiped out; makers widen spreads or hedge to compensate. Inventory skew (more buys than sells or vice versa) is a measurable microstructure signal of directional pressure.

title: Cross-Exchange Arbitrage and Fragmentation
content: The same asset trades at slightly different prices across venues due to fragmentation; arbitrageurs buy cheap on one exchange and sell dear on another, converging prices. In crypto, cross-exchange and cross-chain arbitrage is a persistent source of volume and a key reason prices stay aligned. Latency, withdrawal fees, and bridging costs determine how tight the band stays.

title: Emission Cliffs and Inflation Narratives
content: Token emission schedules define how supply grows over time. Steep early emissions create inflation cliffs that suppress price, while 'low float high FDV' launches sell a small float against a huge fully-diluted valuation, setting up unlock cliffs of sell pressure. Reading the emission curve tells you when dilution hits the market and whether the schedule aligns with protocol revenue.

title: Unlock Schedules and Sell Pressure
content: Vesting and unlock calendars determine when locked team, investor, and treasury tokens become liquid. Concentrated unlocks (a cliff after a lockup period) create predictable sell pressure that markets often price in early. Monitoring unlock calendars and comparing circulating vs total supply is a core tokenomics diligence step for any new listing.

title: Circulating Supply Reporting Manipulation
content: Projects can report a small 'circulating supply' to inflate market cap per token while holding the rest in escrow, or count locked tokens as circulating to hide dilution. FDV and market cap diverge wildly when supply definitions are manipulated. Cross-checking reported supply against on-chain balances and contract mint/burn logic is standard diligence.

title: Treasury Management Risk
content: A protocol treasury holds reserve assets (stablecoins, native tokens, other positions); concentration in the native token or a single stablecoin creates correlated risk. Treasury moves (selling native token, buying back, lending reserves) signal management intent and can swing price. Diversification, transparency, and on-chain custody of treasuries reduce governance and theft risk.

title: Bonding Curve Pricing
content: A bonding curve is a mathematical price-supply function that sets token price from current supply, so early buyers pay less and the curve adjusts as supply changes. Curves are used in fair launches, continuous organizations, and some memecoin mechanics. They are manipulable when liquidity is thin or the curve parameters favor the deployer.

title: Pre-Mine and Insider Allocation
content: Token allocation diagrams reveal who gets the supply: team, investors, treasury, community, and liquidity. Heavy insider allocation (pre-mine, large seed rounds, no lockup) means insiders can dump on retail; fair launches minimize pre-allocations. Comparing allocation with unlock schedules shows whether early buyers and the team are aligned with long-term holders.

title: Token Value Accrual and Fee Capture
content: Tokens accrue value when protocol revenue flows to holders: buybacks and burns, fee-sharing, staking yields, or governance control over treasury. If a token only pays governance votes on a protocol with no revenue, its value is speculative. Analyzing the fee-to-supply ratio and whether fees are captured on-chain distinguishes productive from hype tokens.

title: Wallet Clustering Heuristics
content: Blockchain analysis groups addresses into clusters using heuristics: the common-input heuristic (inputs to one Bitcoin transaction likely belong to the same owner), change-address detection, and behavior patterns (similar gas settings, funding from the same source, interacting with the same contracts). Clustering is probabilistic, not proof of identity, and drives entity attribution for exchanges, mixers, and scammers.

title: Address Reuse and Linkability
content: Reusing an address links every payment it receives and sends into one public history, so anyone can infer balances and behavior. Fresh addresses per transaction preserve more privacy. On the analytics side, address reuse is a gift: it makes clustering and attribution trivially easy, which is why privacy-focused users rotate addresses and privacy chains are designed around it.

title: Dust Attacks and Dust Tracking
content: Dusting sends tiny amounts to many addresses to 'poison' them; if the recipient later combines the dust with other coins in one transaction, an analyst can link the addresses together (or the duster can airdrop and deanonymize via interaction). Analysts also use micro-transfers as tracking beacons to follow fund movement across wallets.

title: Taint Analysis and Fund Tracing
content: Taint analysis propagates a 'contaminated' label from known illicit inputs (hack, mixer, sanction) through subsequent transactions: any output that spends tainted inputs inherits the taint, typically weighted by value. It is the core technique behind tracking stolen funds across chains and through bridges, and its limits (heuristics, obfuscation) matter when presenting findings as fact.

title: Mixers and Peeling Chains
content: Mixers (e.g. Tornado Cash-style zk anonymity pools, or simple coinjoin schemes) break the input-output link of funds. When mixers are unavailable or risky, launderers fall back to peeling chains: a series of transactions that move small amounts through many fresh wallets, sometimes crossing exchanges and bridges at each step. Peeling chains have a recognizable structure analysts detect by wallet-age and step-size patterns.

title: CREATE2 Address Prediction
content: CREATE2 lets a contract be deployed at a deterministic address derived from deployer, salt, and init code, enabling 'counterfactual' addresses that exist before deployment. Analysts watch CREATE2 because scammers pre-compute addresses used for fake mints, airdrops, or hidden token contracts; forensics can identify the eventual deployer by solving the CREATE2 parameters.

title: Transfer Event Log Forensics
content: ERC-20 and ERC-721 transfers emit standardized Transfer(from, to, value) events that block explorers index; they are the backbone of wallet history and token-flow analysis. Because logs are cheap and permanent, forensics reconstruct movement from events rather than parsing every internal call. Tools like Etherscan, Dune, and custom indexers all rely on these indexed topics.

title: Deployer Behavior Fingerprinting
content: Deployer wallets leave fingerprints: funding source, gas strategy, deployment timing, use of specific factories or proxies, and interaction with known scam infrastructure. Rug-pull detection scores tokens by deployer history (prior rugs, fresh wallets, laundered funding). Fingerprinting is probabilistic and needs corroboration with on-chain and off-chain evidence.

title: Multisig Threshold and Signer Monitoring
content: Multisig wallets (e.g. 2-of-3, 5-of-9) protect funds by requiring multiple signatures, but the threshold and signer set determine actual security: low thresholds reduce protection, and a compromised majority of signers defeats the scheme. High-profile bridge hacks succeeded when attackers obtained enough validator/signer keys. Monitoring signer additions/removals and threshold changes is a leading risk indicator.

title: Token Approval Forensics
content: ERC-20 approvals grant another address the right to spend your tokens; infinite approvals (type(uint256).max) persist until revoked. Analysts trace approval events to find which contracts hold spending power over a wallet, which is how approval-drainer scams are reconstructed after the fact. Revoking stale approvals is a standard hygiene step that reduces future exposure.

title: Solana Token-2022 Transfer Hooks
content: Token-2022 is the extensible Solana token standard; transfer hooks let a token enforce custom rules (fees, blacklists, royalties) on every transfer. The same power can be abused: a token can silently block sells or take a fee on every move, a form of programmable rug behavior. Users should inspect a Token-2022 mint's extensions before trusting it.

title: Soft Rug vs Hard Rug
content: A hard rug is an on-chain exit: deployer removes liquidity, disables sells, or mints and dumps. A soft rug is subtler: no code change, but the team manipulates price via wash trading, dumps from insider wallets, or abandons the project while retail holds. Soft rugs evade simple 'liquidity removed' scanners and need behavioral analysis to detect.

title: Honeypot Detection Checklist
content: A honeypot token lets buyers in but blocks sellers, usually via a blacklist or a hidden transfer check in the contract. Detection checklist: verify the contract source (or decompile), check for blacklist/whitelist functions and owner-only transfer gating, test a sell in a fork, and review holder concentration and liquidity lock. Honeypots are the most common memecoin scam on new chains.

title: Wallet Drainer Kit Architecture
content: Drainer kits are off-the-shelf phishing kits (e.g. Inferno Drainer style) that deploy fake dApps and, once the user connects and signs, execute a chain of calls: setApprovalForAll/approve, transferFrom, and sometimes permit signatures. Kits are branded, leased per week, and reused across hundreds of phishing sites, making their wallet addresses and bytecode valuable threat-intel signatures.

title: Approval-Based Drainer Flow
content: The approval drainer flow: victim connects wallet to a fake site and signs an approval (often infinite); the scammer's contract then calls transferFrom to move tokens without any further victim action. Because approvals are off-the-radar until spent, victims only notice when balances disappear. Mitigation: revoke unused approvals, reject infinite allowances, and treat every signature as a transaction.

title: Permit Signature Phishing
content: EIP-2612 permit lets token holders authorize spending with a signed message instead of an approval transaction, so phishing sites can request a harmless-looking signature and then submit it themselves to drain tokens gaslessly. Because the victim never sends a transfer, the theft looks like it came from nowhere. Only sign typed data on sites whose contract and purpose you verify.

title: Metadata and Hidden-Mint Rugs
content: Some token contracts hide a mint function or an ownership backdoor behind an innocuous name, or the deployer changes metadata (name/symbol/supply) after launch to rebrand the token and dump. Hidden mint is detectable in bytecode even when source is not verified; metadata changes appear as ownership transactions. Both are classic signals for a pump-and-dump or slow rug.

title: Pump-and-Dump Orchestration
content: Organized pumps recruit victims in Telegram/Discord, buy a low-cap token in coordinated bundles at launch, then sell into the retail buying wave they create with shills and fake volume. The orchestration is visible on-chain: bundled mint-to-distribution, many small buys from fresh wallets, then rapid distribution to exchanges. Recognizing the launch pattern beats trying to time the dump.

title: Fake Presale and Fake Launchpad
content: Fake presales and launchpads clone a popular project's site and collect 'presale' deposits into a wallet that never launches a token. They exploit FOMO around whitelists and early-bird discounts. Red flags: unverifiable team, no audited contract, deposits to a plain EOA wallet, and social accounts created days before. Verified launchpad contracts and audited sale mechanics are the baseline defense.

title: Deployer History as Scam Signal
content: A deployer wallet's past behavior is one of the strongest rug signals: prior scam deployments, funding from mixers or hacked wallets, brand-new wallet age, and repeated identical token patterns all raise the probability of a rug. Combining deployer history with holder concentration and liquidity-lock status gives a composite risk score before any money is committed.

title: Address Poisoning and Lookalike Detection
content: Address poisoning spams the victim's transaction history with near-identical wallet addresses so a future copy-paste sends funds to the attacker. Lookalike token scams rely on the same confusion: identical name/symbol with a slightly different contract address. Detection combines fuzzy address matching, symbol/ticker similarity scoring, and flagging zero-value 'poisoning' transactions that share the victim's history.

title: Multi-Timeframe Confluence
content: Multi-timeframe analysis reads the same market at several scales (e.g. 15m, 1h, 4h, daily) and trades only where signals agree: a daily uptrend, an hourly pullback to support, and a 15m reversal. Confluence raises the probability of a setup because smaller timeframes inherit the larger trend's momentum. The common error is fighting the higher timeframe for a smaller entry.

title: Elliott Wave Basics
content: Elliott Wave theory models price as a five-wave impulse (three up, two corrective) followed by a three-wave correction, reflecting crowd psychology from optimism to exhaustion. Wave counting is subjective and notoriously easy to retrofit, so it is best used as a framework for probable swings rather than a precise forecast. Labels (1-5, A-B-C) help structure where support and resistance may form.

title: Ichimoku Cloud
content: The Ichimoku Cloud packages trend direction, momentum, and support/resistance into one chart: Tenkan/Kijun lines, the Senkou Span A/B cloud, and the Chikou lagging line. Price above the cloud is bullish, below bearish, and cloud thickness approximates volatility. It is a lagging-indicator system, most useful in trending markets and unreliable in sideways chop.

title: Wyckoff Accumulation and Distribution
content: Wyckoff theory describes markets as cycles of accumulation (smart money buying quietly), markup, distribution (smart money selling to retail), and markdown. The phases are visible in price/volume structure: accumulation shows spring/soar tests and decreasing volume on dips; distribution shows upthrusts after rallies. Identifying which phase a market is in frames whether breakouts are likely to follow through.

title: Volume Spread Analysis (VSA)
content: VSA reads the relationship between price spread (range of a bar) and volume to infer institutional activity: a wide-spread bar on high volume near support often signals absorption and a potential reversal, while narrow spreads on low volume mean the market lacks conviction. It treats volume as the footprint of smart-money participation rather than a standalone oscillator.

title: Breakout and Retest
content: A breakout occurs when price closes beyond a range, level, or pattern; the retest is the return to the broken level, which should now act as flipped support (after a breakout up) or resistance (after a breakout down). A clean retest that holds confirms the breakout; immediate reclaim of the range suggests a false breakout. Volume and candle shape at the retest separate continuation from failure.

title: Gap Types
content: Gaps form when price jumps between sessions with no trades in between. Common gaps fill quickly and carry little signal; breakaway gaps open a new trend and often do not fill for a while; exhaustion gaps appear near trend ends and typically fill fast. In 24/7 crypto the concept applies across weekends, halts, and major listings where continuous markets break.

title: Relative Strength vs the Market
content: Relative strength compares an asset's performance to a benchmark (BTC, ETH, or the sector): an asset making higher highs while the market makes lower highs is showing internal strength, and vice versa. RS is a durable edge filter for rotation and for picking long candidates; it is calculated as price ratio or beta-adjusted return and works across timeframes.

title: Swing Structure: HH/HL and LH/LL
content: Swing structure is the rawest form of trend definition: an uptrend prints higher highs and higher lows (HH/HL), a downtrend prints lower highs and lower lows (LH/LL). Marking the most recent swing high and low defines the invalidation point for any directional thesis. Structure is objective where indicator readings are not, making it the anchor for trade management.

title: Position Sizing and Risk Management
content: Technical analysis is incomplete without position sizing: risking a fixed fraction of capital per trade (commonly 1-2%) keeps a losing streak from drawing the account down. Stop placement from structure (below the swing) plus risk-per-trade defines size; expectancy (win rate x avg win - loss rate x avg loss) is what makes a system profitable over time, not any single setup.

title: Account Abstraction (ERC-4337)
content: Account abstraction turns wallets into smart contracts, enabling features impossible for EOA wallets: social recovery, spending rules, batching, gas sponsorship, and passkey/session keys. ERC-4337 standardizes this without consensus changes by using a user-operation mempool and entry point contracts. It broadens the attack surface too (signature validation bugs, malformed user ops), as Trail of Bits audits of smart accounts have shown.

title: Rollup (Optimistic vs ZK)
content: A rollup executes transactions off-chain and posts compressed data to a base chain (e.g. Ethereum), inheriting its security. Optimistic rollups assume validity unless challenged during a fraud-proof window; ZK rollups post cryptographic validity proofs that are immediately verifiable. Rollups change the fee and latency economics of DeFi and introduce bridge/withdrawal delays that matter for arbitrage and MEV.

title: Bug Bounty Program
content: A bug bounty program pays whitehat researchers to find vulnerabilities before attackers do, typically with a severity-graded reward table and scope limits. In Web3, Immunefi-style platforms host most major programs and have become the de-facto safety net between audits: 92% of critical Web3 vulnerabilities are reported through the top platform. Bounties complement audits, which are point-in-time snapshots.

title: Liquid Restaking Token (LRT)
content: A liquid restaking token represents a claim on restaked ETH that is also actively validated for other networks (AVS), letting holders earn restaking yield while staying liquid. LRTs add layers of delegation and operator risk on top of normal staking; slashing events or AVS failures can reduce the underlying value. They are a major TVL category in modern DeFi.
